We came across a bullish thesis on Molina Healthcare, Inc. on Valueinvestorsclub.com by banjo1055. Since the thesis was published on June 6th, MOH shares have pulled back as lower membership and elevated medical costs pressure earnings, creating a near-term hurdle even as improving Medicaid rates may support a turnaround. In this article, we will summarize the bulls' thesis on MOH. Molina Healthcare, Inc.'s share was trading at $199.46 as of October 27th 2026. MOH's trailing and forward P/E were 2.44k and 20.48 respectively according to Yahoo Finance. This isn't the first time we see a health insurance company pitched as a great investment. MOH shares gained 24.44% over the last 12 months. Comparable stocks like Elevance Health and UnitedHealth Group gained 25.31% and 15.52%, respectively, during the same period. Why are health insurance stocks rising so much and is it really a good time to buy them? In June, we published an article about the 7 Best Turnaround Stocks to Buy in 2026 and MOH ranked #3 in that article. MOH has gained modestly since then, leaving investors waiting for the turnaround to deliver stronger returns. This article highlights MOH among 10 value stocks legendary investor Seth Klarman is buying in 2026. Before getting into our analysis, let's take a look at the business and why some investors like the stock so much. Molina Healthcare, Inc. (NYSE:MOH) is one of the largest Medicaid-focused health insurers in the country, with about 7% of the national Medicaid market. While most competitors spread across Medicaid, Medicare, and commercial insurance, Molina focuses almost entirely on Medicaid, which makes up about 90% of its members and 75% of its premium revenue. Read More: 15 AI Stocks That Are Quietly Making Investors Rich Read More: Undervalued AI Stock Poised For Massive Gains: 10000% Upside Potential The stock has fallen more than 50% since October 2024 as rising medical costs squeezed profit margins across the industry and raised concerns about future membership losses. Even so, the bullish argument is that Molina's low-cost structure could still let it hit its 2029 earnings target of $25 per share, well above the $17.35 Wall Street currently expects, and at a valuation far cheaper than its historical average. Molina's edge comes from being built specifically for Medicaid rather than juggling multiple insurance businesses. This focus helps it manage costlier patients more efficiently and negotiate better deals with healthcare providers. That advantage shows up in the numbers: Molina keeps medical costs meaningfully lower than peers and runs one of the leanest overhead structures in the industry, despite being smaller than its biggest rivals. To hit its $25 earnings target, management is betting on a broad Medicaid industry recovery, alongside Molina's own margins improving, though staying below its historical norms. If weaker competitors keep struggling, Molina could gain market share as those rivals pull back. The company has also built a track record of buying underperforming Medicaid plans cheaply and turning them profitable, a strategy that has historically delivered strong returns. Molina's own earnings target implies the stock could be worth significantly more than where it trades today, with further upside possible if Medicaid margins recover closer to historical levels. On the other hand, if industry pressures persist and profitability doesn't improve, earnings and the stock's value could fall well below current levels. In short, the stock's outcome is closely tied to where Medicaid margins ultimately settle. The biggest risk is that new federal rules under the One Big Beautiful Bill, including stricter work requirements and more frequent eligibility checks, could shrink Medicaid enrollment meaningfully over the next decade. Molina believes it can offset these losses by winning new contracts and making acquisitions, including a major recent win managing Florida's Children's Medical Services program. That Florida contract is notable because it covers medically complex children, generating premiums far higher than Molina's typical member. It reflects Molina's ability to win specialized, higher-value Medicaid business, and further contract wins or a pullback by weaker competitors could support future growth. Ultimately, the debate on Molina comes down to whether today's Medicaid headwinds are temporary or a lasting shift for the industry. If margins recover, the path to the company's ambitious earnings target looks achievable; if pressures persist, that recovery could take longer. Another risk for the stock is that regulatory capital requirements limit the cash available for acquisitions and share buybacks. Molina's insurance subsidiaries must retain minimum capital buffers, so their cash cannot automatically be transferred to the parent company. State regulators also restrict the timing and amount of these transfers. Molina contributed $439 million to its regulated subsidiaries in 2025 to support their capital requirements. If additional funding is needed, more cash could remain committed to the health plans rather than support expansion or shareholder returns. This means improving earnings would not necessarily produce the same increase in freely available cash. In our opinion, the recovery thesis becomes less attractive if capital requirements constrain the acquisitions and buybacks that could support per-share earnings growth. Hedge fund positioning shows a cautious signal for MOH (see why Diamond Hill Capital sees long-term value in MOH after recent pressure). As per our database, 51 hedge funds held Molina Healthcare, Inc. at the end of the first quarter, down from 55 the previous quarter, suggesting institutional investors have been trimming exposure amid ongoing Medicaid uncertainty. By comparison, Centene Corporation (NYSE:CNC) was held by 72 hedge funds, down from 78, Elevance Health, Inc. (NYSE:ELV) was held by 87 hedge funds, up from 78, and UnitedHealth Group Incorporated (NYSE:UNH) was held by 130 hedge funds, down from 145. Elevance Health, Inc. stood out as the only peer to see rising institutional interest, while the broader group, including Molina Healthcare, Inc., saw funds pull back. Short interest data also paints a fairly concerning picture for Molina Healthcare, Inc. relative to its peers. About 6.70% of Molina Healthcare, Inc.'s float is sold short, well above Elevance Health, Inc. at 2.65%, Centene Corporation at 2.44%, and UnitedHealth Group Incorporated at 1.74%. This suggests Molina Healthcare, Inc. is drawing more skepticism about its near-term recovery than Elevance Health, Inc., Centene Corporation, and UnitedHealth Group Incorporated, with bearish bets against it remaining considerably heavier than those against all three peers. MOH's forward P/E is 20.48x. Elevance Health, Inc., UnitedHealth Group Incorporated, and Centene Corporation trade at forward P/Es of 14.39x, 17.64x, and 12.42x, respectively. MOH's own forward P/E was 10.45x on December 31, 2025, making its current multiple approximately 96% higher, although weaker earnings estimates can increase the ratio without improving investor sentiment. We believe the current valuation requires confidence in an earnings recovery despite rising medical costs, reimbursement uncertainty, and potential Medicaid membership losses. However, the premium to all three peers appears demanding given that Molina's margin recovery remains unproven. Management's 2029 earnings target of $25 per share is approximately 44% above the $17.35 analyst estimate cited for that year, demonstrating the gap between the bullish scenario and prevailing expectations. We believe MOH needs measurable improvements in underwriting margins and sustainable earnings to justify its current valuation, rather than relying on its long-term target alone. If Molina protects its cost advantage and converts new contracts into stronger profits, its premium could become justified, but the current valuation offers limited room for disappointment and we would prefer a lower entry price. Previously, we covered a bullish thesis on Molina Healthcare, Inc. (MOH) by Long-Term Pick in February 2025, which highlighted Molina's Marketplace growth, new Medicaid and Medicare contracts, $42 billion 2025 premium revenue guidance, and $378 fair value estimate. MOH's stock price has depreciated by approximately 25.17% since our coverage. We believe MOH could be a good long-term investment if its cost advantage drives a sustained Medicaid margin recovery, but its premium valuation makes a lower entry price preferable. Molina Healthcare, Inc. is not on our list of the 40 Most Popular Stocks Among Hedge Funds. title: UNH students scramble to vote after student ID ban. Town clerk explains law. - Seacoastonline.com
content: DURHAM — Massachusetts native Azrael Ross’ plan to vote in New Hampshire for the midterm election Nov. 3 is now up in the air. The University of New Hampshire graduate student now studies and lives in the Granite State. Ross hoped to use her university-issued student identification card in the Nov. 3 election, but she won’t be able to do so after the U.S. Supreme Court’s recent ruling to uphold the state law banning the use of school IDs to obtain a ballot. “I don’t know anything about the Massachusetts midterms right now because I’ve been around people who are from New Hampshire," Ross said in a Monday Oct. 26 interview. "I don’t feel like I have enough time now to go back and vote and participate as I should. It’s tough because I thought I would be guaranteed an ability to vote here." Ross said she has been paying attention to New Hampshire’s races for the U.S. House of Representatives and Senate seats on the ballot, but not those taking place south of the state line. Student IDs were barred at polling places in June, when Republican-backed House Bill 323 was signed by Gov. Kelly Ayotte. The law was enforced during New Hampshire’s September primary election, though it was being challenged in a federal lawsuit by the Coalition for Open Democracy, a Concord-based voting rights organization. In early October, federal Judge Joseph Laplante ruled the law could stay in effect, but that New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan should not have outright prohibited student IDs during voter registration. The U.S. Supreme Court overruled Laplante in a Thursday, Oct. 22 decision, less than two weeks before Election Day, arguing “lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election,” according to the order. Associate Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the lone dissenting justice. With the U.S. Supreme Court having spoken, Durham town clerk Rachel Deane stated the general election will proceed similarly to how the state primary ran, though with a larger student turnout expected. “Durham is incredibly focused on making sure that anyone who is truly qualified to vote gets to vote,” she said. Out-of-state students must bring proof of identity, domicile, age and citizenship to the polls in order to vote. An out-of-state driver’s license suffices for the age and identity portion, while a rental or lease agreement or utility bill can be shown to prove domicile in Durham. The New Hampshire secretary of state has posted all the requirements. UNH has also posted voting information for students. Deane noted election officials will accept students who provide electronic proof of domicile by showing their on-campus housing assignment through the University of New Hampshire’s Webcat portal. A U.S. passport or birth certificate is accepted for proof of citizenship. Students without either can fill out a qualified voter affidavit in their place attesting to their citizenship. Volunteers in Durham’s election will be trained for all potential voting scenarios involving students. “We’re prepared to assist any student that has no other form of ID to troubleshoot how they can actually proceed with voting,” Deane said. Durham officials said students can vote with government identification and proof of New Hampshire domicile. But students interviewed at UNH aren’t confident most of their peers will make it to cast ballots. Ross and members of her social work program cohort commented on the high court's decision. “At that point, it’s so complicated to even be able to get to vote, and now they’re taking away your ability to use the student ID,” said Vivian Eisenmann. “It’s so complex to be able to do something that we’ve been told is one of our rights, but they’re making it impossible. They can’t take away the right to vote but they can take away all the accessible options to vote.” “There’s never any situation where we should be reducing people’s accessibility to voting. It should always be about increasing people’s accessibility to voting,” Elle Legard added. The student voter identification issue has been debated and litigated in New Hampshire for years. Durham Town Administrator Todd Selig began his tenure in town in 2001. The “highly politicized” topic was spoken about before he arrived at Town Hall, Selig said. “It’s something that I think, generally speaking, on the Republican side, they want to be more strict in terms of allowing college students to vote in the communities where they’re attending college,” he said. “On the Democratic side, they tend to be more welcoming in making it easier for college students to vote in the community they’re attending college.” Deane, Durham's town clerk, anticipates higher turnout at Oyster River High School for the Nov. 3 midterms than during the November 2024 general election. “It’s so hard to predict because these elections seem to be different every year,” she said. Two years ago, over 8,300 votes were cast, with the town reporting nearly 2,500 same-day voter registrations, according to the town. Legard and fellow UNH graduate student Max Murdach will be offering students free rides to the polls on Election Day. Murdach said he works six jobs on and off in addition to his studies. “I have a very busy schedule but I have the offer out there to people,” Murdach said. During the primary election, Legard estimated she drove about 20 students to Oyster River to vote. The master's student is preparing to encounter students who hoped to vote but may not have the necessary identification. “Why are we limiting students’ access to influencing policies that dictate how we live and exist in this community? It’s just wild,” she said.

This article walks through what the filing shows, how the insurance and Optum units each contributed, what the balance sheet and cash flow looked like, and which uncertainties remain as the company heads toward year-end. The report was issued weeks before today's date, and it remains the most recent full set of results from the company. UnitedHealth Group released quarterly results in October and furnished the full earnings release to the Securities and Exchange Commission. Revenue came, a touch below the reported in the same quarter of last year. Over the first months of the year, revenue totaled. Earnings from operations climbed from a year earlier. The company's chief executive, Stephen Hemsley, said in the release that the quarter reflected discipline and execution across the organization. That is a management characterization, and the filing's tables remain the better guide to what actually changed. The medical care ratio, which measures the share of premium revenue spent on patient care, improved in the same quarter last year. For an insurer, a movement of that size is large, because each percentage point on a premium base of this scale represents a very large amount of money. The release states that the ratio included favorable development of prior-period reserves. That detail matters for interpretation. Favorable reserve development means that medical costs for earlier periods turned out lower than the company had estimated, and the benefit is booked in the current quarter. It is real accounting earnings, but it is not a measure of how current-period claims are trending. The operating cost ratio also improved, indicating that administrative spending fell relative to revenue. Together, the ratios explain most of the jump in operating earnings. Market participants typically watch the medical care ratio because insurers set premiums months in advance and then absorb whatever utilization arrives. Elevated use of outpatient procedures, specialty drugs and behavioral health services pressured the industry in recent periods, so a lower ratio is read as evidence that repricing and benefit changes are working. Whether the pace of improvement can continue without the reserve benefit is a question the company did not fully answer in the release. In the release, the company lifted its full-year guidance for this year. The phrase at least signals a floor set by management, not a ceiling, and it is guidance and not a reported result. That arithmetic reflects normal seasonality in insurance, where medical costs generally rise late in the year as members reach deductibles, and it also reflects the non-recurring nature of some quarter benefits. The change in guidance came with a set of operating commitments laid out in the same document. The company said it is aiming to eliminate of its current prior authorization volume by the end of this year, and that it will pass through manufacturer drug rebate discounts to clients in full by the start of in earlier years. It also said earnings on individual Affordable Care Act plans would be eliminated and rebated members this year. Those commitments are best read as part of a broader effort to respond to public and political scrutiny of the insurer. They carry costs and may reduce certain revenue streams, and the company has not detailed every financial effect. UnitedHealthcare, the insurance arm, reported revenue, down, while earnings from operations rose. Medical membership ended September, compared with in June and a year earlier. The open question is how much of the loss is intended pruning and how much reflects customers moving to competitors, and the release does not quantify that split. That swing is among the most notable lines in the report, since Optum Health was a source of pressure when the company reset its expectations earlier. Detail stands out in the pharmacy unit. Adjusted prescriptions fell, which the company tied to membership declines at UnitedHealthcare and at other customers. Lower volume in the pharmacy business is the mirror image of lower insurance membership. Cash generation was solid in the quarter. Cash conversion net earnings is generally read as a sign that reported earnings are backed by actual cash. The debt-to-capital ratio edged up at the end of the quarter. The company said it is aiming to bring that ratio by year-end, which implies that debt reduction is a stated priority for the coming months. Capital was also distributed to stock owners through channels. Year to date, the company spent on its share retirement program and on dividends, according to the release. For a company of this size, those amounts are meaningful, although they compete with the stated goal of lowering leverage. The combination of rising leverage, a large dividend, and an active share retirement program is worth watching. If medical costs surprise to the upside, the cushion provided by cash flow would be tested first, and the company would have to balance its commitments against the ratio goal it has publicly set. XTB market commentary published in October reported that UnitedHealth Group shares gained after the stronger-than-expected earnings and the higher guidance. Pulse Two, a financial news site, similarly highlighted the guidance raise and the operating earnings. The reaction fits a pattern seen in large managed care names during this reporting season, when results that show falling medical cost ratios tend to be rewarded. Still, a gain in a stock of this size can be a move worth many in market capitalization, so it should not be dismissed as small. Price moves after earnings reflect many factors, including what Wall Street research desks had assumed beforehand, the tone of the management call, and positioning ahead of the report. None of those can be separated cleanly from the published figures, and the stock's path since the report depends on factors beyond the quarter itself. The latest report is evidence of stabilization, not proof that the volatility is behind the company. First, the reserve development benefit flattered the medical care ratio, and the underlying trend may be less favorable. Second, membership is shrinking in the segments that provide the largest premium base, and a smaller base can limit revenue growth next year. Medicare Advantage payment rates, member-scoring methods and audit activity are set or enforced by federal agencies, and the company has repeatedly said that such decisions affect its plan design. Medicaid redeterminations and state budget pressures add another layer of unpredictability for the community and state business. These moves could improve trust among patients, doctors and lawmakers, but they may also trim margins. Finally, the pharmacy benefit business operates under regulatory and legislative scrutiny over how rebates and fees are structured. The company's pledge to pass through all manufacturer rebate discounts by the start of in earlier years is a response to that scrutiny, and its financial effect will only become clear as the transition proceeds. Managed care companies have spent the past years working through higher utilization, tighter government payment, and rising specialty drug costs. UnitedHealth Group's quarter fits into that shared story but also stands apart in scale, because it combines the nation's largest commercial and Medicare Advantage insurance book with a very large physician, data and pharmacy services arm. That structure has advantages and complications. Optum's services provide diversification and data that can help manage costs, but they also create conflict-of-interest questions that lawmakers and regulators have raised. Competitors with narrower insurance-only models face fewer of those questions, while lacking the same breadth. In the quarter, the company's medical care ratio and operating margin at UnitedHealthcare show recovery, but both are still modest by the standards of the company's history before the recent stress. Peers reporting this season have also described a mix of stabilizing costs and ongoing caution, and readers should check each company's own filing for exact figures. Sector context matters because the healthcare industry is exposed to the same federal decisions. A change in Medicare payment rules or drug pricing law would not affect insurer in isolation, and results across the group can move together on such news. The next scheduled milestones include the quarterly report, which the company typically issues in January, and the annual Medicare Advantage enrollment period that opens in the fall. Enrollment trends in that window will show whether the benefit and price changes made for next year attract or deter members. Other items to follow are the progress toward the debt-to-capital goal, the pace of the share retirement program relative to debt paydown, and any further disclosure about the size of favorable reserve development. A quarter in which reserve benefits played a large role makes the underlying trend in the coming quarters more important. The earnings release, furnished as an exhibit to a Form eight-K, describes revenue that was roughly flat to slightly lower than in the same quarter a year earlier. That is a notable statement for a company that normally grows its top line, and it is explained by deliberate choices: membership fell in several products, and Optum Health stepped back from markets where it did not have enough value-based care presence to run the model well. Despite the flat revenue, earnings from operations rose sharply and the net margin improved. Both generally accepted and adjusted earnings per share moved higher than in the prior-year quarter. Operating cash generation was strong relative to net earnings, which is the kind of conversion that long-term holders of insurer stock tend to watch because it indicates that reported earnings are turning into cash rather than sitting in receivables or reserves. The balance sheet commentary was measured. The ratio of debt to total capital edged up from the previous quarter, but the company reiterated its aim of reaching roughly two-fifths by the end of the year. It also continued to pay dividends and carry out its share capital program, which signals that management sees the financial position as stable enough to keep rewarding equity owners while it works the leverage ratio down. Readers should keep in mind that favorable development of prior-period medical reserves helped the quarter. Reserve releases are legitimate, but they are also a reminder that part of the improvement reflects estimates from earlier periods turning out better than expected, not purely new-quarter performance. The medical care ratio compares the money the insurer pays out for patient care with the premiums it collects. For a business whose premiums are largely fixed at the start of a plan year, a small move in that ratio can swing earnings dramatically. During the difficult stretch before this report, the ratio had worsened as utilization rose, especially among older members, and as certain outpatient and specialty services cost more than priced. In the third-quarter release the ratio improved year over year. Management credited cost management, benefit and pricing changes, and care delivery initiatives. In practical terms that means plan designs were adjusted for the current year, some unprofitable counties or products were trimmed, and the company pushed harder on coordination of care so that fewer patients reach expensive settings unnecessarily. The operating cost ratio also improved, although the release candidly states that the company is spending more on technology, artificial intelligence enabled operations and staff. That is a useful nuance. Efficiency gains are not coming only from cutting spending; some of the cost base is being redirected toward tools meant to speed up claims, documentation and payment accuracy. Because the ratio can be influenced by the mix of members, seasonality and the timing of reserve changes, it rarely tells a complete story in one quarter. Market participants therefore compare it across several periods, and they watch how management explains the contribution of reserve development versus underlying medical trend. UnitedHealthcare is the insurance operation that offers employer plans, Medicare Advantage, Medicare supplement and Part D, and Medicaid managed care. In the quarter its revenue declined slightly while earnings and margin rose. That combination is the signature of a business pruning less attractive membership and repricing what remains. Membership shrank in employer, Medicare Advantage and Medicaid categories. The release points to employer attrition and to changes in Medicaid eligibility as drivers, both of which are largely outside the insurer's direct control. Medicare and Retirement revenue fell because of membership and product mix, which fits the company's earlier decision to exit plans and regions where benefits could not be supported by the payments received from the federal program. An important dated reference point for the Medicare Advantage business is the quality rating system, commonly called Stars. Management said the results for the coming plan year were in line with expectations and showed improvement on many quality measures. Star ratings influence bonus payments and marketing advantages, so a result described as in line removes one unknown rather than adding a surprise. The competitive context includes other large insurers such as CVS Health through Aetna, Elevance Health, Humana and Cigna, all of which have been recalibrating Medicare Advantage offers. UnitedHealthcare is the largest participant, which makes its choices about benefits and county footprints influential for the whole industry. Optum Health is the care delivery arm, including primary care clinics, multispecialty groups, ambulatory surgery centers and value-based arrangements in which providers are paid for keeping a defined population healthy. Revenue there fell meaningfully in the quarter, and the release attributes this to exiting markets where the company lacked sufficient value-based care presence. At the same time, earnings in the unit rose sharply from a level near breakeven. Management linked the improvement to operational discipline and to better medical cost management. For a care delivery business that depends on paying clinicians and facilities while bearing some of the medical cost exposure, the move away from near-breakeven performance is a meaningful signal that the restructuring is starting to take effect. The logic of shrinking to improve is straightforward. Value-based care works best with density: enough patients in a region that clinicians can coordinate, share data and spread fixed costs. Where density is thin, the unit economics are harder, and a decision to exit can raise average performance even as revenue declines. Readers should treat the revenue decline as intentional and look at whether earnings per patient keep improving. The stakes are high because Optum Health is also tied to the Medicare Advantage strategy. When UnitedHealthcare membership changes, the number of patients flowing into Optum clinics changes too, so the two businesses must be managed together rather than as separate silos. Optum Insight supplies data, analytics, revenue cycle tools and technology services to hospitals, physician groups and health plans. Its revenue grew modestly in the quarter and earnings increased, which management tied to new product offerings and efficiencies. The release highlights artificial intelligence tools for clinical documentation and for payment accuracy, an area where automation could shorten the time between a patient visit and a properly adjudicated claim. Optum Rx, the pharmacy benefit business, saw revenue roughly flat while earnings rose. The release credits growth in biosimilar adoption and operational gains. Prescription volume declined, mainly because of membership losses in UnitedHealthcare, a reminder that the insurer and pharmacy businesses move together because many Optum Rx members arrive through the health plan. Pharmacy benefit managers have been under intense scrutiny from lawmakers, employers and state attorneys general over rebates, spread pricing and the opacity of net costs. Against that backdrop, the company said it is moving toward a fee-based, transparent pharmacy model. Competitors include Express Scripts from Cigna and Caremark from CVS Health, and all three have been pressed to adjust how they are paid. The combined message from Insight and Rx is that Optum is trying to be seen less as a collection of intermediaries and more as a set of technology and service tools whose value can be measured. Whether customers agree is something upcoming contract cycles will reveal. Alongside the financial statements, the release lists several commitments that respond to criticism from patients, physicians and policymakers. The most visible is a step to reduce prior authorization requirements. Management said that by the end of the year it intends to eliminate about three-tenths of prior approval volume. Prior authorization is the process in which a clinician must obtain insurer approval before certain services or drugs, and it has been blamed for delays in care and for administrative burden on physician offices. A second commitment concerns manufacturer drug rebates. The company pledged to pass through the full amount of rebates it receives to clients by a stated year later in the decade. It also said it is rebating earnings on individual plans offered under the Affordable Care Act for the current year. These are unusual statements for a large insurer, and they show the degree to which public pressure is shaping corporate behavior. A third commitment is financial and philanthropic: one billion dollars directed to the United Health Foundation, focused on rural, maternal, child and behavioral health. The pledge is large, though it is spread over time and is separate from operating results. None of these items is a certainty about how events will unfold; they are announced intentions. Their real impact will depend on how clinicians, employers and regulators experience the changes, and on whether the company can maintain medical cost discipline while making approvals easier. Chief executive Stephen Hemsley framed the quarter around discipline and execution. In the release he said the company aims to deliver a simpler, more supportive experience for patients and the clinicians who care for them. The emphasis on simplicity echoes the broader theme that a complicated structure, many overlapping programs and uneven execution contributed to the earlier troubles. The release also describes governance changes. The board created a Public Responsibility Committee, named a new lead independent director and added a new independent director. Committees of this type are meant to oversee issues such as patient access, public trust and societal impact, which have moved from the periphery to the center of the insurer's reputation. Governance changes are easy to announce and harder to evaluate. Market participants usually look for evidence in how often the new committee reports, how it interacts with management and whether the board is willing to challenge strategy. The addition of an independent lead director can provide a counterweight, particularly while the company is under regulatory and political scrutiny. For readers, the key point is that the quarter included not just numbers but also structural signals. Those signals reinforce management's argument that the reset is organizational as well as financial, though the final judgment rests on sustained performance. The first uncertainty is medical cost trend. Utilization among older members, the cost of specialty drugs and the pace of outpatient procedures all affect the medical care ratio. The improvement reported in the third quarter is welcome, but a single period does not settle whether the underlying trend has stabilized. The role of favorable reserve development in that improvement is another reason for caution. The second is membership. The release acknowledges decreases across employer, Medicare Advantage and Medicaid. Some of this is deliberate, but shrinking membership can reduce scale advantages in negotiating with providers and pharmacies. The upcoming annual enrollment period for Medicare Advantage will offer a fresh signal about how benefit changes are received. The third is regulation and public scrutiny. Federal agencies, congressional committees and state regulators continue to examine Medicare Advantage coding practices, pharmacy benefit management and prior authorization. Commitments made in the release may help the company's standing but cannot remove those inquiries. The fourth is execution of the Optum restructuring, particularly the balance between exiting markets and maintaining care continuity for patients. Each of these items is a matter of expectation rather than fact, and the company's own guidance language includes the usual caveat that results can differ from what management anticipates. Full-year guidance was raised, with generally accepted earnings per share expected to be at least a stated floor and adjusted earnings per share at least a somewhat higher floor. The wording matters: both are phrased as minimums, which leaves room for the final figure to be higher but also reflects that only one quarter remains. Because the figures reflect results through the third quarter, much of the full-year number is already locked in. What the release does not do is supply a detailed bridge for the final quarter. Readers cannot determine from the document alone how much of the remaining quarter is expected to come from underlying improvement and how much from the timing of reserves, portfolio gains or seasonal patterns. For a Medicare-heavy insurer, the fourth quarter often brings higher utilization as deductibles are met, so seasonality is a real factor. It is also worth remembering that guidance is a management statement of expectations. It is not a promise, and it is subject to the same medical cost, regulatory and economic variables that affected earlier quarters. Careful readers compare the language in the release with the more detailed discussion in the later quarterly filing and with remarks made on the conference call. The most reliable source is the earnings release itself, filed as an exhibit on the company's Form eight-K at the Securities and Exchange Commission. A companion supplemental document in the same filing presents the figures in a more tabular layout. The company also publishes an announcement of its earnings date through a wire service, which confirms the timing and the conference call details. Other helpful primary sources include the quarterly report on Form ten-Q, which carries detailed notes on reserves, legal matters and segment results, and the annual report, which describes the business model and the main uncertainties in depth. Exchange quote pages provide a convenient place to follow the company's trading symbol and corporate actions. Third-party commentary can be helpful for context, but readers should always compare it with these primary sources, because summaries can omit nuance or misstate details. title: Meet UNH’s New AD, Ryan Colton - The New Hampshire
content: The stadium seats are filling, the student section is cheering, and the band's sound carries across the field on a crisp Saturday in Durham. As fans gather to watch the Wildcats take the field, a new face becomes a familiar presence in the stands: Ryan Colton, the University of New Hampshire’s (UNH) new athletic director. In July 2026, UNH’s President, Elizabeth Chilton, appointed Colton to lead the university’s 20-sport NCAA Division I athletic program. From Saturday football games to winter hockey games, Colton’s role extends far beyond the playing field, encompassing the student-athletes, campus community, and the fans who make up Wildcat athletics. Before arriving in Durham, Colton spent eight years at the University of Richmond in Virginia. His career in athletics administration also includes time at the College of the Holy Cross and Providence College. But his path to athletics leadership was not a conventional one. Colton studied political science at Bucknell University, where he also played quarterback for the football team. It was there that he developed a passion for intercollegiate athletics. After graduating, Colton attended New England Law in Boston and worked as a practicing attorney for several years before making the transition into athletics administration. “While I worked hard with long hours in both [Law and Athletic Administration], I really had a passion for intercollegiate athletics and the impact it can have on young people and the campus and broader community,” Colton said. “For me, this has really been a labor of love; I really do love coming to work every day.” Now, as he settles into his new role at UNH, Colton is focused on strengthening the connection between athletics and the broader university community. He wants student-athletes to be involved beyond their prospective teams and sees opportunities for athletics to bring students, faculty, and residents together. “I love working with colleagues across campus, whether it be in the president's office from deans to professors, on ways we can all collaborate to better support not just our student-athletes but also our students across campus,” Colton said. “I want to give a really great student-athlete experience, but also, how can our sports better improve the experience for all students across the board and the pride across the institution?” A central goal of Colton’s is the “whole-student athlete” experience. For him, supporting student-athletes means looking beyond their performance on the field or court. Academic achievement, personal growth, and a sense of belonging are also important parts of their college experience. Colton also hopes to strengthen the sense of community among UNH’s athletic program, encouraging teams to support one another and using sports as a way to build pride across the university and throughout New Hampshire. Balancing the needs of 20 different sports can be difficult, but Colton approaches the responsibility by focusing on the people behind each program. As he reflects on his belief that the value of college athletics extends beyond competition, he attends as many games as possible to show his support for student-athletes and coaches. The commitment has quickly become a family affair. Colton’s wife, Brittany, and their two children, Grady and Ella, have joined him in embracing their new Wildcat community. Ryan Colton and his wife Brittany, son Grady and daughter Ella at his introductory press conference on Aug. 11, 2026, in the Service Credit Union Victory Club. (Photo Credit: Alex Miller/UNH Athletics) “My daughter has fallen in love with volleyball,” Colton said. “This is really a family endeavor for me; my family is completely immersed in Wildcat athletics now.”

title: UNH leading effort to strengthen U.S. seafood supply through aquaculture - NBC Boston
content: Roughly 80% of the seafood Americans eat is imported, but a University of New Hampshire-led initiative is aiming to boost U.S. aquaculture — the farming of fish. Do you know where your seafood comes from? According to NOAA, roughly 80% of the seafood Americans eat is imported. Researchers at the University of New Hampshire are leading a major new effort aimed at growing more seafood domestically through sustainable aquaculture. Stream NBC10 Boston news for free, 24/7, wherever you are. Just a quarter mile off the coast of New Castle, UNH researchers are raising steelhead trout in a floating sea farm known as an Aquafort. It’s become a model for studying ways to make seafood production more sustainable. “We are growing fish at a very small community scale for the purpose of supplementing the seafood markets within the local area. So, the difference between wild-caught fish and aquaculture fish are hatched from eggs Our fish are actually hatched at a local New Hampshire hatchery up in Ossipee,” said David Fredriksson, director of UNH’s Center for Sustainable Seafood Systems. About 4,000 steelhead trout are taken to the floating pen, where they're raised for several months before harvest. The fish share the pen with sugar kelp and mussels. Researchers say those species act as natural biofilters, helping recycle nutrients and maintain balance within the ecosystem. The approach, known as integrated multi-trophic aquaculture, is designed to make seafood farming more environmentally sustainable by raising multiple species together. Fredriksson said his interest in aquaculture stems from a desire to build a more resilient domestic seafood supply. “I firmly believe that we need to make a change and we need to make a change with data, with science,” said Frederiksson. "We feel that with the data approach, we can do this in such a responsible way where we can reduce the effects of imported seafood coming into our markets." The goal, he said, is not to compete with local fishermen but to provide additional products to local seafood markets. "The only thing that we're competing with is imported salmon, which is a good product, but it's imported " Fredriksson said. "Can we do that at home with our own people? That's what I'm passionate about." Researchers hope to replicate similar small-scale sea farms in coastal communities around the country, tailoring each operation to local environmental and economic conditions. That effort recently received a major boost. UNH was selected to lead a new NOAA-supported initiative focused on strengthening America's seafood supply through aquaculture research. The NOAA Cooperative Institute Fostering Aquaculture Research and Markets (CIFARM) brings together research institutions from across the country to study ways to expand domestic seafood production. “The CIFARM is taking this type of model and adapting it to go to these other regions in the United States and start out small,” said Michael Chambers, research professor, Center for Sustainable Seafood Systems at University of New Hampshire. “Since this is a national effort, we want to cover all the exclusive economic zone waters of the United States. So, for example the UNH, their tentacles reach out into the Pacific Ocean to other islands such as American Samoa, Guam, Saipan, all the way down to University of Miami, their tentacles reach to the Caribbean, so USVI, and Puerto Rico, the Gulf and the West Coast and the Northeast so we have this expansive realm of experts to mobilize and expedite aquaculture in the US quickly. We’re just getting going now. We have a lot of work to do.” Locally, Chambers says the Aquafort provides an educational opportunity. “We bring people out on a weekly basis to look at what we do and not be afraid of what we do. As we build out these other farms we hope to do the same thing.” He said it's an opportunity to discuss the environmental impact of imported fish. “I would much rather eat fish from my backyard than bringing it from halfway across the world. Imagine the carbon footprint on that product that’s coming on in.” At the New Hampshire site, the team raises and distributes about 20,000 pounds of steelhead trout annually to local businesses, including Richard Pettigrew's seafood market in Portsmouth, Seaport Fish. "Having a local product right here that we can get pretty much on demand when they're harvesting to add to our product list is huge," Pettigrew said. He says consumers love buying a fish with a local backstory. “It’s just a New Hampshire-raised fish the whole way through,” said Pettigrew. "When you're buying aquaculture product, you can definitely tell if there's been love put into it.” Some of that locally raised trout also finds its way to community organizations, including Gather Food Pantry. The fish is smoked and packaged ready to eat. “By being able to offer something like the trout, we feel that just feeds into our mission of providing like food equity and dignity,” said Tania Marino, Deputy Director of Gather Food Pantry. “We have a lot of demand from our local unhoused population who don't have access to any cooking facilities. So for them to be able to come in and grab one of these pouches of this trout that's not only delicious and very nutritious, but something that they can just take and eat directly from the pouch is really valuable for them. Our older adults who are unable to cook for themselves anymore, they love it so much.” For pantry leaders, the partnership provides access to nutritious local food that might otherwise be out of reach. "It's very meaningful for us to be able to provide food," said Marino. "When we're able to say, 'Take home some steelhead trout,' it's not just a pouch of fish. It's a pouch of goodness and nutrition and love." Researchers hope efforts like these can demonstrate how aquaculture can support local economies, improve food access, and help strengthen the nation's seafood supply for years to come. title: UNH Jackson Estuarine Lab Expansion Opens in Durham, NH - Hoodline
content: The University of New Hampshire cut the ribbon this week on a $5.2 million expansion of its Jackson Estuarine Laboratory, a research outpost on Great Bay that has been studying New Hampshire's coastal waters since 1970. The new 4,500-square-foot addition brings dive lockers, boat storage and a dedicated meeting space to a facility perched on Adams Point, about five miles from UNH's Durham campus. UNH held the ribbon-cutting ceremony at the laboratory on Great Bay, according to the New Hampshire Union Leader. U.S. Sen. Jeanne Shaheen joined UNH and state leaders at the event, the paper reports, marking a milestone for a lab that was among the nation's first academic facilities dedicated solely to studying estuaries. Great Bay itself is sometimes referred to as New Hampshire's hidden coastline, and the lab also studies the Hampton-Seabrook estuary further south. Shaheen called the laboratory's work “indispensable to advancing research on coastal ecosystems in New Hampshire and around the world,” per the Union Leader's reporting, and said the upgraded facility will support breakthroughs in building resiliency in estuarine and coastal systems. The senator helped secure more than $3 million in federal funding for the project, though a separate 2023 announcement from her office described $3.8 million heading to UNH to launch what it called a state-of-the-art water quality lab — the two figures were not reconciled in the available record. The addition includes a dedicated space for community partners and collaborators, a 36-person meeting room with an adjacent office, and a new entryway, according to the Union Leader. It also adds two high bays for working on vessels, buoys, and aquaculture and remote-sensing equipment, plus dive lockers with showers and room to store and repair scuba gear. The station already keeps three 19-foot outboard-powered center console boats on hand for fieldwork, per the UNH School of Marine Science and Ocean Engineering, and the building and its adjoining greenhouse run on full seawater capability year-round. Erik Chapman, director of UNH's School of Marine Science and Ocean Engineering and N.H. Sea Grant, said the project modernizes and expands the nearly 60-year-old laboratory and increases UNH's capacity for research, teaching and public service, the Union Leader reports. The Turner Group handled architecture and engineering for the project at an estimated cost of $5.2 million, while Tighe & Bond provided civil engineering and Milestone Construction took part in building the addition. The National Institute of Standards and Technology funded the expansion, with UNH contributing additional funding, and a second phase of renovations to the original building is still planned. The laboratory will serve as the permanent home of the Piscataqua Region Estuaries Partnership and is set to host community collaborators including N.H. Fish and Game, the N.H. Department of Environmental Services, The Nature Conservancy N.H., and the Northeastern Regional Association of Coastal Ocean Observing Systems, according to the Union Leader. UNH also plans to provide a new minivan to improve collaborator and student access to the site across disciplines. That collaborative footprint matters because the bay itself is under strain. Eelgrass acreage in the Great Bay Estuary has faced decades of decline and took a significant drop in 2025, according to the Piscataqua Region Estuaries Partnership. In response, PREP this year launched Great Bay's first seed-based eelgrass restoration effort, holding reproductive shoots in flowing seawater tanks at the Jackson lab. PREP and its partners collect more than 1 million data points annually to gauge the estuary's health. Water-quality data gathered through the lab's network show just how variable conditions in the bay have become. The Great Bay National Estuarine Research Reserve found that heavy winter precipitation lowered spring salinity in 2024, while a prolonged summer and fall drought pushed the estuary into high-salinity conditions, with measurements peaking at 31 parts per thousand in October of that year. Nutrient concentrations followed a similarly erratic pattern, running high through spring before hitting historic lows in summer and late fall, the reserve reported. The reserve's monitoring program is designed to track those kinds of shifts, identify new threats and measure whether management efforts are working. Its staff monitors saltmarsh health annually and works with partners to track mudflats, eelgrass and oyster beds — part of a System-Wide Monitoring Program that all 30 National Estuarine Research Reserves nationwide use to collect comparable data. The reserve also operates four water-quality stations and a weather station in coordination with the Jackson lab, while PREP sponsors additional monitoring stations, a coastal watershed data portal and a periodic State of Our Estuaries Report. UNH President Elizabeth Chilton said marine science and sustainability are longstanding strengths at the university and that UNH is committed to expanding its impact, according to the Union Leader's account of the ceremony. Chilton added that the expansion creates opportunities for students to work directly alongside scientists and gain hands-on experience. Research and monitoring tied to the laboratory focuses on water quality, environmental toxins, habitat restoration and aquaculture, and UNH frames that work as delivering economic and quality-of-life benefits for Granite Staters. The lab's reach extends well beyond New Hampshire's coastline. Estuaries, where rivers meet the ocean in partially enclosed brackish water, serve as sheltered spawning and feeding grounds that support nearly 70 percent of the nation's commercial fish catch, per UNH's marine science school. They also absorb floodwater and blunt the force of storms to protect property. Federal agencies including the EPA, U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, Army Corps of Engineers, USGS and NOAA all rely on the Jackson lab in their coastal resilience work, and local collaborators range from individual coastal towns to regional planning offices and groups like the Conservation Law Foundation and The Nature Conservancy. Over more than five decades, research tied to the laboratory has covered oysters, lobsters, horseshoe crabs and eelgrass, deepening understanding of coastal ecosystems, environmental quality and the links between watersheds and human health, according to UNH's marine science program. The facility also facilitates investment supporting New Hampshire's emerging aquaculture industry. With the new high bays, dive lockers and meeting space now in place, UNH officials say the Durham lab is positioned to keep expanding that body of work on a changing bay. title: Why Some Plants Grow Where Others Cannot - University of New Hampshire
content: Alders can thrive in soils that are inhospitable to other plants. Whether due to environmental changes, human-initiated uses, or some combination, the capacity for New Hampshire’s lands to sustain plant life is continually evolving. New Hampshire Agricultural Experiment Stations scientists at the University of New Hampshire are discovering new ways that land with harsh, inhospitable soils and environments across the Granite State could be stewarded toward healthier, more productive conditions that support the state’s forests, natural resources, and food systems. The key has been understanding the relationship between microbes and fungal communities in soils near “pioneer” plants, which are able to grow where other plants simply cannot. Anyone who has battled weeds encroaching on driveways or patios knows that certain plants find a way to grow in unexpected places. Sometimes, however, environmental disruptions can be too harsh for just about any plant, such as in old landfills, strip mine or gravel pit sites, and areas where soil is salty or has been eroded. That’s where actinorhizal plants—plants including alders as well as bayberry, sweetfern, avens, and others that partner with nitrogen-fixing bacteria—gain a competitive advantage. For example, after Mount St. Helens erupted the first plants to repopulate the devastated countryside were actinorhizal, providing the natural first step toward restoration. “It’s imperative to understand how the pioneer plants’ microbiomes change over time at different locations and in relation to environmental disturbances and contaminants,” says Station scientist Louis S. Tisa, professor of microbiology and genetics in the department of molecular, cellular, and biomedical sciences. “That knowledge will provide the foundation for successful and lasting partner-planting and bioremediation efforts at ecologically damaged sites like landfills, or even the 22 superfund sites in New Hampshire.” Pioneer plants such as alders (Alnus rugosa) often play vital roles in land reclamation projects. To better understand why, Tisa and Alexandra Gomez ’G27, a doctoral candidate in microbiology in the UNH College of Life Sciences and Agriculture, studied microbial characteristics in bacterial and fungal communities within alder root nodules, immediately next to the roots, and in the surrounding soil across six different New Hampshire sites during every season of a three-year research period. In a paper chosen as an Editor’s Pick in Applied and Environmental Microbiology, Gomez and Tisa showed that the root nodule and soil microbiomes vary in different locations—from pristine rural freshwater wetland site to those located near major roadways and subject to vehicular exhaust and contaminant runoff—underscoring the importance of understanding environmental and soil variables for land reclamation. While not as inhospitable as some environments, New Hampshire roadside soils are exposed to salt, metals, water-soluble chemicals from asphalt, exhaust byproducts, and other contaminants. Of the six sites studied, five were near roadways but differing in other respects. The sixth site, in Candia, was rural, near to freshwater peatlands and far from any roadways. In addition to proximity to a roadway, the Hampton site was next to a saltwater marsh, the Durham site was close to a freshwater wetland, the Epping site was urban, the Durham-adjacent site was wooded, and the Raymond site was near a highway but not water. “Alex did a really good field study and picked the locations well,” says Tisa. “We were able to see interesting differences in the microbial populations among the sites, reflecting the different environmental conditions and seasonal variability.” The study’s findings show that the microbial populations in and around the alder root nodules were different from site to site, and they also showed seasonal variation. The Candia site had the lowest overall bacterial diversity, perhaps because the high levels of aluminum and sulfur in the soil, typical for peatlands, selected for certain species. The nitrogen-fixing bacterium Frankia also dominated the bacterial populations within the Candia alders’ root nodules. At the roadside sites, high levels of soil zinc strongly shaped the microbial communities. The relative amount of Frankia varied between the roadside sites, with the Epping and Hampton sites having the highest relative nodule occupancy. Another important factor shaping the microbial populations was soil moisture, as the three sites with the most Frankia had more consistent water sources than the Raymond and Durham sites. Drought also played a role in one of the years. Typically, Frankia relative abundance peaks with high summer photosynthesis rates, but a spring and summer drought in 2022 pushed peak abundance from July to October region-wide. Nitrogen fixation within the root nodules and alder viability may therefore be limited in areas with insufficient soil moisture. title: UNH holds memorial for hockey player killed in wrong way crash - WFSB
content:
WEST HAVEN, Conn. (WFSB) - A hockey player police said was killed in a wrong way crash was remembered by the university for which he played. Ryan O’Shea, 21, was hit by the wrong way driver on I-91 south in North Haven on Oct. 16, according to police. The driver, 31-year-old Guillermo Carmona-Lopez, remains in the hospital. The University of New Haven said he was returning to its campus following a game. His legacy was honored at a ceremony, which ended with a plaque in his honor being unveiled. It bears his name in the heart of the campus. “It was really just heartbreaking to see someone so innocent like that just lose a life in such a horrible way,” said Aidan Dowsett, a UNH alum and friend of O’Shea. He described O’Shea as selfless and positive. They stayed close despite only spending a year on campus together. “It really just shows what type of person he was. Even at 21 years old how many people you could touch it’s truly amazing,” he added. “He kind of fit the ethos of the university of New Haven which is ‘Care for the human good.’ He really put himself, you know, behind and put others first,” said Devon Crosby, Director of Athletics, University of New Haven. A scholarship fund will help others follow in O’Shea’s footsteps. To date, more than $55,000 has been raised. “We’ll always be saying Ryan’s name for years to come,” added Crosby. “…obviously nothing amounts to him actually being here, but we’re going to try our best as alumni as a community to remember him as much as we can," said Dowsett. The hockey team plays its first home game since O’Shea’s death Friday night at 8:00 p.m. against Wentworth. A full house is expected for the contest. title: UNH Student Represents New Hampshire in Miss America Competition - University of New Hampshire
content: Lauren Plank ’27 competes in the Miss America competition. (Photo credit: Katrina Bernard Photography) Lauren Plank ’27 would love to tell you she remembers every detail from the moment she was named Miss New Hampshire, earning herself a spot in the Miss America competition she used to watch at home with her mother every year growing up. Details, though, are a little hazy, lost in the surprise of the moment. But what she does remember is feeling like a lifelong aspiration had officially been realized. “When my name was called for the title, I had extreme tunnel vision. I feel like everything around me went blurry and I was feeling shocked and a little bit in disbelief,” Plank says. “Being named Miss New Hampshire was a dream come true. I worked so hard to prepare for this competition, mentally, physically, and in my community, so seeing that work all pay off in that one moment was incredible.” Getting to stand on the stage as part of the Miss America competition in West Palm Beach, Florida, this fall was equally awe-inspiring for Plank. It was a decidedly different vantage point than the one she had as a child, sitting on the couch with her mother watching the event each year. “I’ve dreamed of going to Miss America for as long as I can remember. To be there, involved and competing, still feels surreal,” Plank says. Some of the most rewarding takeaways for Plank were the bonds she built with her fellow competitors. Through a daunting schedule of rehearsals and long days with little rest, the 52 contestants grew close and still talk almost daily in a group chat. The communication major’s journey to the Miss America stage truly began in the summer of 2024, when she entered two local pageants but didn’t earn a title. She returned to UNH for the school year, but the experience was never far from her mind. In 2025, she tried again and was named Miss Bedford, winning $10,000 in scholarship money. In April, after a weeklong competition, she was crowned Miss New Hampshire 2026. The honor was especially meaningful for Plank, who has found a home in New Hampshire after coming to UNH. She initially thought she wanted to attend a big school somewhere far away from her home in Marlborough, Massachusetts, but as decision time loomed, she realized she felt more comfortable staying within easy driving distance of her family. “Deciding to come here was definitely the best decision that I could’ve made,” Plank says. When she found out she would be competing in Miss America, she says she was “so excited to represent the state that I’m furthering my education in.” That relationship to UNH is something Plank expects to be lifelong. She met her best friends here during her freshman year, found a sisterhood at Alpha Chi Omega, and loves cheering on the Wildcats during football season. And she doesn’t envision any of that Wildcat spirit diminishing when she graduates. “Everyone who goes here is a Wildcat for life,” she says. Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. title: UNH Marks Jackson Estuarine Laboratory Expansion at Ribbon-Cutting - University of New Hampshire
content: U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen (with scissors) cuts the ribbon on UNH’s Jackson Estuarine Laboratory expansion with School of Marine Science and Ocean Engineering Director Erik Chapman (to her right), UNH President Elizabeth Chilton (to her left), Jackson Estuarine Laboratory Director David Burdick (to Chilton's left), and state and community partners. New Hampshire’s estuaries and coastal economies are about to get even healthier, thanks to a major expansion at UNH’s Jackson Estuarine Laboratory on Great Bay. At a ribbon-cutting ceremony Oct. 26, 2026, U.S. Senator Jeanne Shaheen joined UNH and state leaders to celebrate the completion of the project, which added 4,500 square feet of enhanced facilities for studying estuaries. “The work done at the University of New Hampshire’s Jackson Estuarine Laboratory has been indispensable in advancing critical research that allows us to better understand our coastal ecosystems in New Hampshire and around the world,” says Shaheen. “I was proud to help secure over $3 million in federal funding to improve the state-of-the-art lab and ensure it has the resources it needs to continue its groundbreaking work, and it was great to see the facility improvements behind this project earlier today. I know this upgraded facility will lead to new breakthroughs for building resiliency in our estuarine and coastal systems. I can’t wait to see all that lies ahead.” “Marine science and sustainability are longstanding strengths at UNH, and we're committed to building on that expertise to make an even greater impact in New Hampshire and beyond. This expansion represents an important investment in that work,” says UNH President Elizabeth Chilton. “Just as importantly, we're creating new opportunities for students to work alongside experienced scientists and gain hands-on experience addressing real-world challenges.” Visitors to Jackson Estuarine Laboratory tour the new facility, including its high bay. Among the features of the Jackson Estuarine Laboratory (JEL) expansion: Two high bays for working on vessels, buoys, and equipment for aquaculture and remote sensing; Dive lockers with showers and space for storage and repair of SCUBA equipment; “This project modernizes and expands UNH’s nearly 60-year-old laboratory on New Hampshire’s Great Bay, elevating UNH's capacity for estuarine research, teaching, and public service,” says Erik Chapman, director of UNH’s School of Marine Science and Ocean Engineering and N.H. Sea Grant. “Research and monitoring focused on water quality, environmental toxins, habitat restoration, and aquaculture deliver direct economic and quality-of-life benefits for Granite Staters.” JEL will also serve as the permanent home of the Piscataqua Region Estuaries Partnership and will host community partners and collaborators — including N.H. Fish and Game, N.H. Department of Environmental Services, The Nature Conservancy N.H., and the Northeastern Regional Association of Coastal Ocean Observing Systems (NERACOOS) — in dedicated space. A new minivan will increase access for collaborators and for UNH students in a range of disciplines. A second phase of the project will involve renovations and updates to the original building. Built in 1970 and located on Great Bay in Durham, five miles from the UNH campus, JEL was the one of the nation’s first academic labs dedicated solely to studying estuaries. Research at the lab helps understand, protect, and manage New Hampshire’s estuaries — Great Bay, sometimes called New Hampshire’s “hidden coastline,” and the Hampton-Seabrook estuary — and advances the state’s coastal economy. Research at JEL, spanning oysters, lobsters, horseshoe crabs, eelgrass, and more, has improved our understanding of coastal ecosystems, environmental quality, and the connection between watershed and human health. Estuaries, partially enclosed bodies of brackish water where rivers meet the ocean, are among the most productive habitats on Earth. They provide sheltered spawning and feeding grounds and are habitat for nearly 70 percent of the U.S. commercial fish catch, and they absorb flood water and mitigate the effects of storms to protect property. Total cost for the Jackson Estuarine Laboratory expansion is estimated to be $5.2 million. Funding for the project is from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), with additional funding from UNH. The Turner Group (Concord) were architects and engineers, Tighe & Bond (Portsmouth) provided civil engineering, and Milestone Construction (Concord) managed construction. title: Meet the UNH student transforming foam and fabric into Halloween magic - The Charger Bulletin
content: While some graduate students rest during their free time, Kahlea Hsu spends hours in the campus makerspace carving giant foam blocks into creations. Hsu starts her day at 8 a.m. and doesn’t leave until 10 p.m. She balances graduate school and serves as the dance captain and costume chair for the university’s K-pop dance group, Charger K-pop Dance Crew. Growing up, Hsu’s mother designed group costumes for the family to wear. When her mother stopped after high school, Hsu took matters into her own hands. She entered a performing arts school surrounded by a constant flow of creativity, where Halloween was not a holiday to be missed. “I went to LaGuardia in Manhattan, and you know, everybody was performing arts, everybody there was creative as hell, and Halloween was a big thing,” Hsu said. “You didn’t dress up, you were weird, you were the odd one out.” Hsu began experimenting with special effects makeup, and transformed herself into things such as a cracked doll and a devil costume with a split jaw and large teeth. By her freshman year, her skills had increased so that she could create makeup simulating an injury with a hanging eye. What got Hsu started was a costume depicting a Clicker, a blind, mutated zombie-like creature with a fungal growth covering its head from the video game and HBO series, “The Last of Us.” The detailed costume earned her recognition when the franchise’s official Instagram account featured her work on their story. “In terms of how something looks and how accurate it is the actual thing, I think the Clicker has been my favorite,” Hsu said. “It got recognized or at least the Instagram for The Last of Us. They put it on their Instagram as a story, and I thought that was pretty cool.” Driven by a desire to improve, Hsu created an even more ambitious project the following year: a massive Freddy Fazbear suit, the iconic animatronic bear from the horror video game franchise, “Five Nights at Freddy’s.” “So I ended up making this giant suit that I guess got a lot of attention on campus and I was like, ‘Oh wow, I can do this,’” Hsu said. Following Freddy, Hsu engineered a dinosaur costume that proved to be an intense technical challenge that included an internal framework of PVC pipes jerry-rigged with zip ties and topped with heavy upholstery foam. Hsu designed the head of the dinosaur to pivot and look up and down using a Home Depot bucket lid mechanism. The weight however, caused the structure to collapse. “It was a mess,” Hsu said. “The dinosaur cost the most and we just ended up throwing it out.” Hsu spent as many as 14 hours a day making the costume. She estimates it took about 300 hours to complete. “I really only spent 30 minutes walking around on campus, it was a rainy day, and it was really heavy and the pieces weren’t fitting together so I just, it had to go,” Hsu said. But the 300 hours of work weren’t a waste. The experience allowed Hsu to work with more tools in the makerspace. She worked alongside other students to learn mechanical movement and weight distribution to assist her in future projects. “I didn’t like the dinosaur, but I learned structural things,” Hsu said. “I learned how heavy the materials should and shouldn’t be. Now I can translate the errors and mistakes that I made in that into a new project and go ‘Okay, well I learned a skill from this and I made a mistake in this, how am I going to change that?’” she said. After graduating last semester and leaving the dinosaur behind, Hsu is back at the university as a forensic technology graduate student. During the summer, she spent time working in the New York City morgue, an environment that inspired her next creative project. The idea came during a car ride, where she connected her time spent around real dead bodies at her summer job with her upcoming return to campus. “I was like ‘Wait, I’m going back to school. Zombie, what can I do?’ And then I was like, ‘Oh! Charlie, Charlie’s a mascot,’” Hsu said. The result is her current project: a decomposed version of Charlie the Charger, the university’s mascot. For Hsu, the creative process behind her works begins with a sketch. “Everything starts with a drawing for me,” she said. “I don’t really think I’m a great drawer like an artist-ish. Sketching. I don’t think I’m that great at that, but to me that’s the easiest part of all of this. If I can’t do that, I can’t do this.” After sketching her designs, she starts brainstorming materials to use. To make the heads for her costumes, the process involves gluing foam blocks together and then shaving the material down to the desired shape. For Charlie, Hsu took the original round shape of a head and shaved it down to mimic the elongated features of Charlie. “I kind of just see something and I’m like, ‘How can I mimic it?’ I think I’m pretty good at essentially copying things,” she said. “So it terms of the armor for Charlie, I just kind of saw a picture of it and I was like, ‘Okay, well it’s a piece here and a piece here, and I just need to hot glue it.’” While she holds a passion for crafting, her focus still remains on her academics. “It’s definitely making sure you know what you need to do at what point and to also know that this stuff, the costume stuff, doesn’t really matter.
